prose_evidence.text_as_printed: Without his song, the bard is nothing. Many factors go into a song including component selection, rest selection, instrument usage and your current situation. There are 1,586,991,541,162,320 UNIQUE song combinations . Only about 50-70 of those are actually worth using. Let’s first begin by discussing basic song composition.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: Let's first look at the various components of a Bard Song. Depending on your level you will have between 1-7 Song Component types titled Melody, Embellishment, Lyric, Chorus, Verse, Bridge and Coda. Each of these song component types will have between 1-3 slots available for a single component.. All together, at Level 50, you will be able to mix and match up to 16 separate components each having an cost of between 2 – 9 energy per second. The more components you use, the more energy your song will cost per second. It is important to note that the majority of our song components WILL STACK with each other. In other words, you can put 3 Mellarien's Harmony of War in a song for a "triple effect". It is better in most situations to focus your song in such a way (using multiple same components) as opposed to mixxing and matching individual components. In some cases, components do not stack (or stack for a lessened effect) and those will be addressed individually in a later section.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: Song components pulse once every four seconds. Many song components are persistent so they do not have an effect that fades. Harmony of War for instance will add 12-20 pts of damage for the entire duration of the song without any 4 second pulse effects. However, Bard Regen Songs will only give a benefit of Health / energy regen once every 4 seconds while having no effect in between. In addition, some songs have effects that will be refreshed every 4 seconds such as our Irion’s Psalm of Shields, which gives a Rune component; if you take damage and the rune fades, it will refresh again on the next 4-second pulse of the song.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: Your natural energy regen (NER) is based on your vitality score. As you increase your vitality you will gain a greater NER. This is a constant number both in and out of combat and does not change. However, out of combat, you will receive additional bonuses to the your regeneration which are unrelated to NER..

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: The second method is that of using Rests. In your song composer, you will find a button that reads “Rests”. By Level 50 you will have accumulated a total of 7 rests ranging in value from 2-12. (2,4,5,7,8,10,12). There is an 8th Rest obtainable at L50 from a mob drop worth 11. By using a rest in your song you will reduce the total cost of the song by the value of the rest. So if you add an 8-pt rest to a song which costs 20 to play, the song will now only cost 12. Rests can be placed into any Song Component Slot with the exception of those of the Melody type (See Below). You can only use a rest one time in a song.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: At Level 1, you will receive Mellairien's Anthem of War (a combat Melody) and a 4 pt Rest. All songs MUST have a component in the Melody slot to be saved or played. Put MAoW in your Melody Slot, put the 4 pt rest in the Lyric slot, give it a name and save it and you will have just created your very first song. Because the cost of MAoW is 2 energy / sec and the rest has a value of 4 points, you will not have a song cost as the rest completely offsets the cost of the melody.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: Let’s discusss song cost in more detail now. As you add more components to the song the song cost tax will also increase. You will be using a combination of your NER (Natural Energy Regen) and Rests to offset this. At L1, a bard begins with a NER of approximately 5 energy / sec. This is significant because it means you can offset up to 5 pts of a song’s cost without using rests. In other words, you don’t actually need that rest at L1 4-pt rest as your NER will cover the cost for you. The important factor however, is that many of our other “non-song” abilities such as mez, charm, shouts, etc… also cost energy.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: A common mistake as you gain more components is to make a song where the total amount of Song Cost is equal to the value of the rests…ie…if your song has a cost of 10, you add 10 pts of rest for a total song cost of 0. By creating songs with a cost of 0, you are completely forgoing your NER and wasting any benefits you may be gaining from Vitality. Therefore, except in cases where energy is extremely precious (lot’s of mobs to Crowd Control for instance), your songs should have a cost that at least equals your vitality’s NER. In addition, it’s ok to exceed your NER as well to create even stronger songs by sacrificing your energy at a higher rate.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: Let’s assume our NER is 8, that leaves us with a song costing 9 energy / sec. With an energy pool of 600, we can play our song for approximately 67 seconds before we run out of energy. If we add a 5 pt rest to an empty lyric slot, reducing the cost to 4 energy / sec, we can now maintain the song for 150 seconds before draining our pool. The important thing to remember when composing songs is that at any given time you may need your energy for Crowd Control and emergency situations. Never let yourself run so dry that you can’t take charge of adds.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: By exceeding your NER and total rest value, you are increasing the potency and effects of your song. Many bards, myself included, have two variations of every song type. One variation has a cost that is equal to or less than our NER. This variation is used when energy conservation is necessary for situations such as crowd control or using shouts. The second variation exceeds the NER by 2-15 pts depending on what I want out of the song. By building a combat song without rests, you boost your parties DPS greatly but for a much shorter amount of time. This is the bard’s version of “burst” damage; pushing out the strongest song possible and burning through all your energy to pay for the effect. A good strategy for this type of song building is to play the high cost song at the beginning of a fight and then as your energy approaches 30% or so, switch back over the low cost song in order to regen.

Each has it's own place in the scheme of things and are generally specialized to certain types of song components. However, in many cases, a mod will affect more than one type of song. In rare cases, you will be able to gain armor or parrying daggers that will have an an instrument mod on it as well. ALL Voice mods discovered have been on armor and there are currently no instrument based voice mods. First we'll look at how instrument mods work and then we'll take a look at the different types and what they are generally used for.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: Instruments are the defining factor of a bard. Without an instrument, many of our song components are simply too weak to bother with using when compared to their cost. When adding the appropriate instrument mod however, the component begins to blossom into a very powerful song. The majority of our song components are actually balanced using a 3.0 instrument mod effect (more on this shortly). Yes, it doesn't seem physically possible to play a guitar and shoot a crossbow at the same time, but that's how it works in Vanguard. Through the usage of macros, specifically the /remove and /wear macros, you can quickly and easily switch between instruments and weapons as needed in order to optimize your effects. Keep in mind, the instant you remove your instrument, the song will revert to a lesser version. Likewise, when adding an instrument, the effect is also instant in all but a few circumstances. One exception to the 2H rule is Voice Mods. Symbiotes are created by the Blood Mage by using his own blood and organs harvested from enemies, and subsequently cast on allies or yourself for various buffs. prose_evidence.text_as_printed: Getting the organs you need can be a bit tricky, so heres some comments and tip. First of all, don’t harvest organs when you’re in a group. You’ll divert your attention from the action and that could prove fatal. Since organs stack (up to 20) go find some mobs (even gray ones will do), and harvest off those by yourself. I find that going into “Sanguine Focus” makes it easier to harvest several organs from the same mob since you wont do as much damage and wont take as much damage while waiting for “Grim Harvest” to refresh (15 seconds). I do this since you can harvest several organs off the same mob – yes, a bear does seem to have 4 brains, 3 hearts and more stomachs than a cow! prose_evidence.text_as_printed: The druid’s damaging abilities all fall under three damage types, Arcane, Fire and Physical. The druid has many “Dots” and many direct damage spells or “Nukes” as I think of them. The druid uses up energy or phenomenon points to cast his or her spells. Some spells are instant cast, some have no cooldown and some don’t trigger the global refresh timer, but none of them have all three of the above. So lets look at them one by one.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: As a soloing sorcerer I would highly recommend that you gear yourself in such a manner as to maximize Spell Damage Focus. The extra 20% damage from keeping SDF maxed will help a great deal with taking down the tougher critters that you will run across. Also, each level, I put 5 attribute points each into intelligence and wisdom and two points each into vitality and constitution. There have been, and will be, continuing arguments and discussion about what is the best way to distribute attribute points each level but I find that having the extra hit points and such from con and the extra regeneration from vitality help me a good bit. I also find that having Fire Barrier, instead of Force Barrier, up while soloing also helps a good bit. The spell haste and possible chance of gaining mana back on a cast just can't be beat. I initially thought that Force Barrier would be the way to go for solo, with the extra ac and such, but then I realized that, as a light armor wearing caster, if a mob got to me I was going to take insane damage anyway so why not use my Fire Barrier and just do everything I could to make sure I never get touched by the mobs. Your mileage may vary.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: These are the formative levels for characters where the player first starts to get used to the skills and abilities that their new sorcerer has. I started off as a Qaliathari Human in the Cliffs of Ghelgad. For your first levels you want to do every quest in the little starting town. There are quite a few and getting to level 6 shouldn’t really be an issue and should only take an hour or two at most I suspect. One of the quests will lead you down the road to the Bayside Outpost and, eventually, to the city of Khal.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: Once you hit level 10 you can travel just a bit to the Southeast of Khal to a little outpost called Neamsong Bunkers. As always, I’d recommend doing all the quests here. There is also a missives board here and you will want to take full advantage of it. Grab all the missives you can and travel around killing the mobs needed. Not only do you get xp and coin for completing a missive but you also get a small scroll looking item in your inventory. Hold onto these and turn them in to the appropriate NPC after you collect 10 scrolls for a chance at a rare item. The item you get won’t always be for your class, and will be a blue item most of the time, but even so you can plop the items up on the broker to make a few extra coins. As soon as you’ve collected 15 silver or so I’d head over to Khal and buy your first mount and pick up some horsehoes, tack, and a saddle bag.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: Once you ding 17 head back to Qalia and take the road west of Khal that leads towards Hathor Zi. You don’t actually want to go to Hathor Zi, or anywhere that there are hostile dark elf guards yet. The place you want to go to is called Evendusk, which is a fortress at the end of the road that leads south out of Hathor Zi. You can get there if you travel South of the mountains that surround the dark elf city. The fortress itself is a circular stone building with large ballista outside. The guards and NPCs here are dark elves, but they are neutral. There is no trainer here, or mailbox or broker, but there is a general goods vendor and, the main purpose of your trip, quests. A lot of quests. Do every quests from every NPC here. Some of the them are quest lines with 3 steps or so that get progressively higher in level. I’d personally shy away from the quest that requires you to kill Tiberian Firebirds – at least until you ding 18. The firebirds are nasty 3 dot mobs that have few hit points, but they’ve got a hellacious fire nuke. I’d personally wait until the birds are dark blue before trying to kill them but, hey, that’s just me.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: Around level 20 the mobs in the area will start to turn light blue, some green. Some of the quests you did would have taken you to the area where there are wolves and trolls that you killed. These mobs are still good around level 20 and I personally stayed in the area and grinded on mobs until I hit 21. prose_evidence.text_as_printed: When I dinged 24 I headed over to the Upside Defense Garrison (you can teleport to upside from one of the NPCs on the Khal docks. The NPC across from the one that can send you to Kojan, New Targonoor, etc). There are a few quests you can do from the gnomes at the outpost (don’t forget to look inside the bunkers!). But, in this case, quests aren’t the main reason you came here. Mind you, doing the quests is great xp but the main reason for your trip is turtles. Yes, turtles. If you travel around the coast to the NE of the garrison you will eventually chunk into an area called Strand of the Ancients. This place is a fantastic. The turtles can be found on the beach in the SoTA chunk. They are the only mobs on the beach, are non aggro, and range in level from 25 to 26. Nuke and blast them to your hearts content, they are great xp. You will easily ding 27 off of these turtles.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: if you get sick of turtles (I did, real fast), a good alternative are the trolls of the road from NT to Three Rivers. There are a bunch under and on top of the rock along the dirt path that leads to the gate to the shore area. They are 3-dot level 24; they are social, but the big thing here is that they have a very short leash if you haven't damaged them. I've found if I hit one with Flame Spear, and immediately start backing up, then snare it with Frostbite, the adds will generally turn back before actually catching up to me. The one I damaged will keep coming. At level 25, these mobs are worth over 2k XP each, where 2-dots that are much higher level (like 28-29) are only 1500 or so.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: At 28 you can start doing the quests and such in the Southwatch area of Thestra, which is west of New Targonoor. I’d highly recommend doing all the quests from the Heartsworn Keep area and, once done with those, start on the missives from Southwatch outpost. The missives here will take you to level 36 no problem. I personally avoided the two missives that require you to kill ghosts and rats. I just didn’t find a large enough supply of them to warrant travelling all the way up the mountain to where the mobs are. There is also a quest that starts from Old Lady Sparrowsong that, in the end, will net you a sweet focus item and necklace. This is actually a series of quests that is, for the most part, soloable. I won't spoil the surprise of how this quest line ends :-)

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: For this level I went back to Southwatch and did more missives there. Once I hit level 38 I took a break from xp-ing and did the Unicorn Mount quest. At level 38 everything you need to kill for the quest is grey (very, very grey in the beginning) so the whole quest is soloable. There was one part (kill ashendreg bugbears at some ruins in the Shrine of the Flame chunk) that I asked someone to come and help me with. I could have soloed this part, because everything was grey, but the mobs you need to kill for the quest are nestled in amongst some 4 dot mobs (sometimes linked together) so, all in all, it was just a PITA to do and I would have had to pick off straggler mobs. Having a partner helped things go smoother and to ease the pain of having to kill 47 mobs at this location. You will also get about 10% xp or so from all the various quest turn-ins so even though the quest is all grey it’s not a total write-off. The quest took about 3 nights to complete. I mainly waited until 38 to start the quest because I knew there would be a lot of travelling and, at 38, you get your Quicksilver Ring which will add to your movement speed and give you spell refresh haste. It will be invaluable when you realize the number of mobs that you will have to grind to complete the mount quest and how much travelling you have to do. I liken this quest to having bamboo inserted under my fingernails. But, the reward - even at a 10 gold cost, is well worth it.

prose_evidence.text_as_printed: When I decided I needed a change of scenery from Dragon’s Backbone I went down to Tar Janishir on the continent of Qalia. There are quite a few quests in this area and I figured that it was about time that I checked them out. When I got there I found that there were, indeed, a large number of quests, most in the level 34 – 36 range. However, I was still able to get more than half a level off these quests. If you are going to solo in this area be very careful because even though, for the most part, the mobs are blue to light blue there are some mobs that can silence and root you! I found this out the hard way. Most notable of these are the bandits that you will be asked to kill for several of the quests. These mobs range from level 34 – 36 and are a mix of 2 and 3 dot mobs. This is also the area where you can do the Starspark line of quests. I have yet to complete the line but, at one point, I was required to kill mobs that spawn in amongst come pretty nasty looking 5 dot cyclopses - so you will need to be careful. Also note that all the named mobs that I found in the bandit camps seem to be partially immune to Freeze and totally immune to Frostbite. You’ll need to be pretty careful if you take on the named. I was noticing, though, that Freeze was acting like a slow on them – not totally immobilizing them but slowing them instead. Frostbite didn’t seem to have any affect on them.
